entries.title: Pope Leo vs. Javier Milei: How political is the pope?
entries.summary: Pope Leo XIV's tour of South America has drawn huge crowds — and a measure of political controversy. Perceived criticism of Argentina's leader, and earlier rebukes of Donald Trump, offer a glimpse into papacy politics.
entries.content:
Argentina

Pope Leo vs. Javier Milei: How political is the pope?

November 10, 2026

Pope Leo XIV's tour of South America has drawn huge crowds — and a measure of political controversy. Perceived criticism of Argentina's leader, and earlier rebukes of Donald Trump, offer a glimpse into papacy politics.

The 2.5 million people lining the streets of Buenos Aires to get a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV on Monday left little doubt as to his influence in Argentina and beyond.

"It's very important for Argentinians, for our unity and, above all, to reaffirm faith in the Catholic Church in this country. Argentina is a country of faith, it's always been so," one attendee told DW of the open air Mass.

"The mood from the public about his visit is overwhelmingly positive," Justin McLellan, Vatican correspondent for the National Catholic Reporter, told DW from Argentina's capital. "I think that people are big fans of Leo."

The previous day, Leo had made a series of remarks which many observers took to be criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei and his strict austerity measures, sweeping cuts to social services and the elimination of thousands of public sector jobs.

Afterward, there were suggestions from some of the president's supporters online that the pope, who is returning to duty just a month after cancer surgery, had overstepped his role.

"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," said Leo, the first US-born pope, on Sunday. He also mentioned those who "despite hard work, nonetheless, struggle to meet their household's needs."

Leo doubled down on the message on a visit to a care home before Monday's Mass, where he preached to millions.

Pope Leo walks soft-power tightrope

"It's clearly targeting, without naming, the different policies that the president has put on recently," Jocelyne Cesari, a professor of religion and politics at the University of Birmingham in the UK, told DW, adding that Leo's words were "carefully calibrated."

Throughout its history, estimated by some at close to 2,000 years, the papacy has been a role with huge, and previously very direct, political power. Pope Innocent III, for example, was widely considered the most important man in the Europe in the late 11th and early 12th century. He wielded power over much of Europe and its monarchies, ensuring each territory was run according to Catholic doctrine.

But in the modern day, that power has softened, with 20th and 21st century popes tending to intervene in a broader sense away from direct party politics and policy.

Leo's commitment to walking that tightrope was tested early in his papacy by US President Donald Trump, an ally of Milei, who called him "WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy" in a social media post in April.

"I do not look at my role as being political, a politician," responded Leo. "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel, which is what I believe I am here to do, what the Church is here to do." It's a familiar stance, said Cesari.

"That's a line that all popes before him have walked. We tend to forget that the pope is the head of the state, is a diplomat and is a voice for more than 1 billion Catholics, so the role has always been political."

Can Pope Leo influence Argentina's election?

Both Cesari and McLellan agreed that Leo and his modern predecessors are keen to avoid party politics but instead offer guidance to the 1.4 billion Catholics in the world.

"The strategy of the pope is to position himself as a moral authority, his role is not just to say 'vote for X or Y.' His role is to say there are some moral teachings that can be applied to social life and communities, but people must make their personal decisions," said Cesari.

With Argentina a majority Catholic country, it stands to reason that the pope's word holds plenty of sway. But the longer-term question is whether Leo's perceived criticisms of Milei make a difference in Argentina's general election in October 2027.

"People want to be drawn close to him [Leo]. I think the visit to Argentina could have an influence in the election in that he's certainly given his support to the Argentine bishops who have been critical of Milei's austerity policies and his cuts to social programs," said McLellan.

"I think that that could have an impact in the election and that it will elevate and raise the voice of the Catholic Church in Argentina."

Milei's battle with Catholic Church

But Cesari is not so sure that being sympathetic to a speech transfers to action at the ballot box. "They may revere and respect the pope. But is not clear that that what he says has a direct impact on individual voters," she said.

"His voice will be heard. But from the studies we have, there is not a clear, direct impact on elections. We know that Catholics do not vote in a bloc and we know that lots of them voted for Milei in 2023, even after he called [Leo's predecessor Pope] Francis the representative of evil on Earth."

Milei, a right-wing libertarian and outspoken critic of the ruling class, has long clashed with the Catholic Church. He also called Pope Francis, a native of Argentina, an "imbecile" in 2020 and accused him of promoting communism. He did, however, find a more conciliatory tone on Monday when he called the late Francis an "exceptional figure" and the "most important Argentine in history."

Leo is, McLellan added, "diplomatic by nature." With Trump and Milei both having taken swipes at the Catholic Church in a time of ongoing geopolitical turmoil, that looks to be a critical papal quality.

entries.title: Japan watches for signs of change in Trump's foreign policy priorities
entries.summary: Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm elections may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan watches for signs of change in Trump's foreign policy priorities

November 10, 2026

Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm election may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific.

With just a week to go before the leaders of the United States, China and Russia are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Japan is closely watching for signs of any shift in Washington's policy toward the Indo-Pacific.

The APEC gathering, taking place this year in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, is scheduled for November 18-19.

Tokyo fears that the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm elections may push him to seek a diplomatic quick win, one he can point to as evidence of his statesmanship but that fails to take into account the interests of Washington's allies in the region.

Tokyo has moved swiftly to try to ascertain the mood in a White House that was left reeling by the results of the November 3 midterm election.

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi held talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris on Monday.

Following their meeting, the Japanese Foreign Ministry released a statement saying that both sides agreed to "further advance security cooperation to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-US alliance."

They also vowed to "maintain close communication" on the situation in the Indo-Pacific, without providing further details.

Why is Japan worried?

"Japan's concern is that with Trump becoming a lame duck in domestic politics, he will use his presidential authorities to shift his focus to foreign policy," said Sebastian Maslow, a professor of politics at the University of Tokyo.

"A US deal with China may provide President Xi [Jinping] the ability to intensify pressure on Japan," he told DW. "With Sino-Japanese relations severely strained, this will put Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi in a difficult position and she will have to reassess how to navigate US-China relations."

Margarita Estévez-Abe, associate professor at Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and an expert on Japanese politics, said Japan fears "a transactional Trump who treats Taiwan as a bargaining chip."

She pointed out that after the May summit with Xi, Trump described US arms sales to Taiwan as "a good negotiating chip with China."

Tokyo is also "frustrated" that Trump has not come to its support over the rare earth export restrictions China imposed on Japan after Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last year, with the Trump administration treating the China-Japan feud as "Tokyo's problem," she said.

Efforts to preserve the geopolitical balance

Furthermore, Japan has concerns about Washington's foreign policy positions toward North Korea and Russia.

"Trump has not damaged the US-Japan alliance the way he has strained NATO, but his outreach to Moscow and Pyongyang worries Tokyo," said Estévez-Abe.

"The US relies on Japan as its main military base in the Indo-Pacific, so it is not in Washington's interest to embolden Russia and North Korea against Japan," she added. "But if American softness does raise the threat to Japan, Japanese trust in the alliance will erode. Japan can only hope that doesn't happen."

Ultimately, Tokyo wants to preserve the geopolitical balance in the region and prevent already strained tensions from escalating further. But Japan is increasingly questioning the commitment of a security and trade partner that has stood by it since 1945.

"Japan's security strategy emphasizes preserving the status quo in terms of defending the liberal international order and containing China's role in the Indo-Pacific," said Maslow. "However, in order to achieve this, Japan has emphasized the role of the US alliance as a cornerstone of its foreign policy and security. The reality still is that Japan has no 'plan B' if the alliance unravels."

Diversifying security partnerships

Efforts to strengthen Japan's military are embedded within the framework of the US-Japan alliance, he pointed out. And while there have been calls for Japan to develop an autonomous defense capability, achieving that in the short term is unrealistic given the limitations of its defense industry and a lack of key resources, including critical intelligence.

Over the past decade, Tokyo has proactively diversified its security partnerships, stepping up defense cooperation with European Union member states and NATO, forging a quasi-alliance with Australia, and joining a range of minilateral frameworks across the Indo-Pacific, including with the Philippines.

This reflects Japan's desire to play a more proactive role in shaping regional and global security, Maslow said.

Tokyo hopes no major clashes erupt in the region for the remaining two years of Trump's term and that Washington's resolve is not tested before a new and "strategically more amenable administration comes in," Estévez-Abe said.

Maslow stressed, however, that "hope is not a strategy" and that Tokyo needs to maintain efforts to protect the alliance and double down by demonstrating its own commitments to security with even greater defense spending and by safeguarding economic security.

entries.title: Bulgaria highway pileup kills 12, dozens injured: PM
entries.summary: At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in a series of crashes caused by thick fog in Bulgaria. Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene for the rescue operation.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria: People killed in massive highway pileup

November 10, 2026

At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in a series of crashes caused by thick fog in Bulgaria. Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene for the rescue operation.

At least 12 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a series of crashes on both sides of a highway in Bulgaria on Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities said.

According to the interior ministry, a bus and truck collided, leading to a pileup on the side of the A1 highway near the southeastern city of Yambol.

Weather conditions believed to be a factor

Speaking to reporters at the site, ministry's general secretary Ministry Lyubomir Nikolov said that fog was likely the cause of the accident.

The regional governor of Yambol Georgi Chalakov, said an estimated 50 cars and trucks were involved in the accident.

Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 10 people “died on the spot” and two others died while being transported to a hospital. She said 46 people were also injured and transported to medical facilities.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who was welcoming European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, cleared his schedule for later Tuesday. Von der Leyen said she would cut her ​visit short.

Focus on rescue operations

Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene on the A1 highway connecting the capital Sofia to the Black Sea city of Burgas.

Chief Inspector ⁠Todor Mishinev from the Yambol Regional Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs ⁠told Nova TV that people were still trapped in their cars at the time of speaking.

"Right now, the priority is rescue operations. Once they are completed, the procedural and investigative actions will be carried out," he said.

The injured were being taken to hospitals in nearby cities, while authorities dispatched two aircraft carrying medical teams and stretcher equipment.

Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures. For orientation, EU average is 43 per million.

Victims say reckless driving, neglected road infrastructure and an inefficient justice system contribute to the country's high number of fatal traffic accidents.

entries.title: India: Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love' released
entries.summary: The book goes through the Italian-born matriarch's journey with one of India's most politically influential families. It has already garnered political controversy, with the ruling BJP accusing her of "whitewashing."
entries.content:
India

India: Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love' released

November 10, 2026

The book goes through the Italian-born matriarch's journey with one of India's most politically influential families. It has already garnered political controversy, with the ruling BJP accusing her of "whitewashing."

A memoir bysenior Congress leader and former party president Sonia Gandhi went on sale on Tuesday, with its pages offering a rare insight by the private politician into how she came from humble Italian origins and went on to become the matriarch of India's most powerful political dynasty —  the Nehru-Gandhi family. 

The book called "Belonging: A Journey of Love" has been published by HarperCollins India.

"Much has been written about my family, but rarely with real insight into who they were, their motivations, their struggles, their very human flaws. I wanted to portray them honestly, as people I knew and loved," 79-year-old Gandhi wrote in The Hindu daily newspaper earlier this week.

Who is Sonia Gandhi?

Born Sonia Maino in 1946 in a small Italian village near Vicenza, she met Rajiv Gandhi — the grandson of India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru — at a restaurant in the United Kingdom's Cambridge city.

The two got married in New Delhi in 1968, when Rajiv's mother and Nehru's daughter Indira Gandhi was serving as India's prime minister.

Nearly two decades later, Sonia would find herself holding her bloodied and dying mother-in-law in her arms following a 1984 assassination that saw Indira's bodyguards shoot her to avenge her suppression of an insurgency that culminated in an army assault, called Operation Blue Star, on the holiest Sikh shrine, the Golden Temple.

Sonia's husband Rajiv Gandhi, a pilot who was propelled into politics after his mother's death, became India's youngest prime minister at 40 years old.

He too was assassinated in a suicide bombing in 1991.

Sonia Gandhi later entered politics, going on to become the longest-serving president of the Congress party.

Sonia Gandhi's book sheds light on India's politically influential Nehru-Gandhi family

The Nehru-Gandhi family gave India three prime ministers. In her book Sonia Gandhi talks about her 2004 decision to not take up the top job as prime minister of the world's largest democracy.

In an excerpt from her book, published in The Indian Express, Sonia said her children — and now senior Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi — had then discussed with her, their mother's possible prime ministership.

"One of them asked me straight out whether I would accept the post, just in case our party pulled off a victory. 'Absolutely not' I'd said, almost indignantly,' the excerpt read.

"Neither Rahul nor Priyanka felt that I should become prime minister. They'd lived through the trauma of their grandmother's assassination and the brutal murder of their father. In their minds, holding that office was intrinsically linked with heightened danger. They looked relieved and I, too, felt lighter, having said my views out loud on the question for the first time," Sonia writes.

Ruling BJP accuses Sonia Gandhi of 'whitewashing'

Sonia Gandhi has said that her memoir is not a "political book" but a "personal" one.

But with the Tuesday launch, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Narendra Modi attacked the Congress veteran.

BJP National spokesperson C R Kesavan said that Sonia Gandhi should have named her book "whitewashing" as he accused the memoir of "sugar coating the historical wrongs perpetrated by the Nehru-Gandhi family."

The book has also been released at a time when the Congress party looks to regain ground against the BJP, with Sonia's son Rahul Gandhi rallying India's opposition parties in a series of protests over the last month.

entries.title: Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion
entries.summary: Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.
entries.content:
November 10, 2026

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

Connections to US evangelical nonprofit in question

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Law guarantees freedom to chose religion

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Spain: Police officer killed in Oviedo after neighborhood dispute escalates with explosion
entries.summary: After security services responded to a shooting, a bomb found in a backpack nearby detonated before it could be defused.
entries.content:
November 10, 2026

After security services responded to a shooting, a bomb found in a backpack nearby detonated before it could be defused.

A national police officer was killed in Oviedo, Spain on Tuesday following an explosion in the Villafria neighborhood. Another is being treated for serious wounds in a nearby hospital.

According to local media, the officers were responding to an escalating dispute between two local families in which a 17-year-old girl was shot by a man early in the morning. She is reportedly expected to recover, though it remains unclear what prompted the attack.

Suspect fled the scene

The two officers — a member of the elite TEDAX explosives unit and a canine handler — approached a suspicious backpack at the scene, which then detonated before it could be neutralized. The canine handler and his dog were both killed. The bomb disposal expert is reportedly undergoing surgery to save his leg.

Police union JUPOL expressed its "deep sorrow and dismay" over the incident. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sent his condolences to the colleagues and family of the deceased, saying he was "deeply shocked."

The area surrounding Rafael Urrusti Street has been cordoned off. Spanish daily El Pais reported that Oviedo Mayor Alfredo Canteli is heading to the scene to try and settle some of the confusion surrounding the attacks. The newspaper also wrote that a 64-year-old suspect, a Spanish national, is still at large. He reportedly has a history of petty crimes. He wife has been detained as part of the investigation.

entries.title: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting
entries.summary: Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.
entries.content:
Poland

Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting

November 10, 2026

Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.

A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital. 

On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office announced a formal investigation. 

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media users to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story. 

Are these genuine images of the attacker?

Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.

DW Fact Check: Fake

In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".

But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.

In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.

Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.

It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated.

One important thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.

More about this and how users used sharpening AI tools here.

Did the shooter sympathize with Ukraine?

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

DW Fact Check: Fake

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.

Another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.

DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

Further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation said it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.

Does the attacker have links to a group that operated in Ukraine?

Claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military company active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts.

DW Fact Check: False

The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.

The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variation of this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

This is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.

Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

entries.title: DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for 'cowardice' in conflict with FRN rebels
entries.summary: Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for 'cowardice'

November 10, 2026

Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charges of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,

Major Dieudonne Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.

What is the FRN?

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).

The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu. 

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."

entries.summary: The presidential candidate put forward by the conservative bloc has said she won't meet with the far-right AfD. Meanwhile, Chancellor Merz is set to host Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: President candidate Aigner to meet parties in Bundestag

Published November 10, 2026last updated November 10, 2026

The presidential candidate put forward by the conservative bloc has said she won't meet with the far-right AfD. Meanwhile, Chancellor Merz is set to host Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar. DW has more.

  • Merz is hosting his Hungarian counterpart Peter Magyar in Berlin

Keep reading for the latest news and analysis from Germany on Tuesday, November 10, 2026:

Skip next section Woman sentenced to life in jail over murder of 8-year-old boy

Woman sentenced to life in jail over murder of 8-year-old boy

The district court in Rostock, in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, has found a 30-year-old woman guilty of the murder of an 8-year-old boy and sentenced her to life in prison.

Gina H. had been in a relationship with the boy's father and saw the child as an obstacle to the continued relationship with the man.

According to the prosecution, in October 2025, the accused lured the boy to a nearby pond where she stabbed him to death. She then tried to burn the body to cover up the crime.

It was, in fact, Gina H. who notified police of the body after first claiming to have come across it while walking the dog. She has consistently pleaded not guilty to the crime.

Prosecutors said that despite ending the relationship ending in August last year, the defendant and the boy's father were again in a relationship, with him caring for her horses while she was in pre-trial detention.

The story garnered national attention and sparked outrage when it first broke. Long queues had formed in front of the court ahead of Tuesday's sentencing.

Skip next section UPDATE: Hamburg suspected shooter found dead in hotel room

UPDATE: Hamburg suspected shooter found dead in hotel room

Following earlier reports of a shooting in Hamburg's HafenCity, police have now reported that the 68-year-old suspect shot himself in a hotel room.

"There are indications that the circumstances surrounding the crime may be related to family matters. Our homicide division has been notified and is taking over the investigation," police said on WhatsApp.

Police in southern Germany are now looking into whether the shooting in Hamburg has some connection with two bodies that were found on Tuesday morning in the town of Eningen unter Achalm, to the south of Stuttgart.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Nmecha celebration reopens faith and inclusion debate at Dortmund

IN DEPTH: Nmecha celebration reopens faith and inclusion debate at Dortmund

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

Read DW's full story on Nmecha's celebration and the fallout it has had.

Skip next section Merz urges EU financing plan for Ukraine support until 2034

Merz urges EU financing plan for Ukraine support until 2034

The German chancellor has called on Germany's EU partners to contribute fairly to closing the gap in Ukraine's financing.

Merz's request came in a letter written to the president of the European Council, Antonio Costa, in which he also indirectly threatened to block other financial issues if the EU's member states refuse to heed his call.

The chancellor said an agreement on support for Ukraine was "an essential prerequisite for resolving this problem and for discussing further issues, particularly those with financial implications."

"Support for Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and this must also apply to burden-sharing in providing that support," he added, urging Costas to make the issue a top priority for the EU summit set to take place in Dublin on Friday.

Currently, some €45 billion ($50 billion) are missing to meet Ukraine's financial needs as it fends off continued Russian attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in October that his country needs €70 billion, of which the EU has pledged half.

Merz is aiming to secure more financing from EU partners to share the load, with the issue likely to come up in his meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Tuesday.

Skip next section AI could replace 800,000 jobs, employment agency head says

AI could replace 800,000 jobs, employment agency head says

Andrea Nahles, the head of the German Federal Employment Agency, has said some 800,000 jobs could be lost to AI in the next 15 years, but added that an equal number would be created thanks to the new technology.

"We predict that over the next 15 years, about 800,000 jobs in Germany will be lost due to AI, but a similar number will also be created," Nahles told the Handelsblatt newspaper.

"Some industries will be hit harder by these job losses, such as business service providers and analytical roles at insurance companies and banks. Nevertheless, I would like to see more investment in AI in Germany — but only if it boosts productivity, not just because it's trendy."

Skip next section UPDATE: Hamburg shooting suspect still at large — report

UPDATE: Hamburg shooting suspect still at large — report

According to media reports, heavily armed Hamburg police were deployed following reports of shots being fired in an apartment just 100 meters (around 330 feet) away from the Elbphilharmonie.

Ambulances were also deployed to the scene.

Police have not yet commented on the background of the incident, but two injured people are believed to be a man and a woman. The man had reportedly been shot in the hip while the woman was suffering from a neck wound.

The suspected shooter had not yet been apprehended, according to the Hamburger Abendblatt. However, a police spokesperson said they posed no danger to the general public.

Skip next section 37 years after fall of the Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans today?

37 years after fall of the Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans today?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

DW asked three artists about their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

Skip next section Large police presence in Hamburg's HafenCity

Large police presence in Hamburg's HafenCity

A large number of police have been deployed to the HafenCity / Am Kaiserkai area in Hamburg, close to the famous Elbphilarmonie, according to a post by Hamburg police on X.

It wasn't immediately clear what the cause of the deployment was, but the police said two people had been injured.

German media reported that the injuries were the result of a shooting.

We will bring you more updates as they come.

Skip next section Wadephul skeptical of Russia ahead of Abu Dhabi talks

Wadephul skeptical of Russia ahead of Abu Dhabi talks

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has expressed doubt over Russia's willingness to genuinely enter into negotiation talks to end the war in Ukraine.

"Is Russia truly willing to negotiate?" he asked. Or, "is this just a negotiating charade intended to distract from the fact that Russia intends to continue a brutal war of aggression, particularly against the civilian population?"

His comments come as representatives from Ukraine and Russia began the first round of talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi. US and European representatives will also be present.

Russia "must finally give up its maximum demands," Wadephul added on the sidelines of a G7 foreign ministers meeting.

Skip next section Aigner to meet with CDU/CSU, Greens and SPD in Bundestag

Aigner to meet with CDU/CSU, Greens and SPD in Bundestag

The top candidate to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president, Ilse Aigner, is set to visit the Bundestag, where she will meet with the center-right CDU/CSU bloc, the Social Democrats and the Greens.

She has said she will not meet with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) after one of their top members called her nomination a "disgrace." She also has not received an official invitation from the Left party.

Aigner was officially nominated by the CDU/CSU bloc, also known as the Union, on Monday, practically securing her future as German president. She already has support from the SPD and Greens.

The official vote will take place on January 30. The president is chosen by the Bundestag. Despite being the highest political office in the country, it is a largely ceremonial role.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from a foggy autumnal Bonn.

The main events planned in Germany today include a visit by the top candidate for the German presidency, Ilse Aigner, to the German Bundestag, or parliament, to meet with political parties.

The other is a reception by Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar in Berlin.

These are both happening against the backdrop of the UN's COP climate conference in Turkey and talks between Russian and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Abu Dhabi.

entries.title: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
entries.summary: From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

November 10, 2026

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.



That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA), which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

What exactly is electrification?

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

Where are we right now with global electrification?

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Are there any limitations to what we can electrify?

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.



In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

What are the benefits of electrification?

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel's energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

Any challenges to electrification?

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity, and electrified demand.

According to the IEA, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (5 to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (1 to 5 years), and EV charging infrastructure (1 to 2 years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.
